hypotheses_validated.claim: Verifier major finding reproduced and root-caused: gen-001's 32-thread tail still followed spin_us because a participant queued behind another process's thread on a different CPU is never reached by the spinners' SwitchToThread, and freshly signalled sleepers get stranded the same way; the dispatch ended only when a spinner hit its deadline or the other thread's time slice ended.
hypotheses_validated.evidence: gen-001 pool, 32 threads, spin_us=1000/10000: p999 305-1010 / 401-1700 us, max 1018-1050 / 2045-8427 us. Instrumented runs (16 busy threads): every 3 ms dispatch had the caller in its spin loop and all workers but one started; the laggard was a just-signalled sleeper (its sleeping flag still set), so excluding sleepers from the stall check left those tails.

hypotheses_validated.claim: Stall rule fixes the tail: a participant that has not picked up the dispatch 20 us after the caller started waiting (200 us when the dispatch had to wake workers) makes the caller and every worker that has seen the dispatch sleep; an idle CPU takes the stranded thread.
hypotheses_validated.evidence: Interleaved A/B, 20000 samples, 32 threads spin_us=1000: gen-001 mean 12.7-16.2 us, p999 305-619, max 1027-1035 us; final mean 6.4-7.5, p999 71.5-71.9, max 194-364 us. spin_us=10000: gen-001 mean 14.0 / max 2045 us; final 7.2 / 138 us. With 16 busy threads (spin 3000): gen-001 mean 95-151 us with 63-82% of the time in >1 ms dispatches; final 54 us, 0-0.6%. A variant without the rule (back-off only) kept 26-68% of the time in >2 ms dispatches; test_pool's stranded check catches it.

hypotheses_validated.claim: When no CPU is idle (every CPU busy with other threads) spinning loses to sleeping, so a slow stall (>0.5 ms to clear) or the waiting caller kept off its CPU >0.5 ms starts a sleep-only back-off (10 ms doubling to 1 s), after which the pool spins again.
hypotheses_validated.evidence: 32 threads + 32 busy threads (spin_us=5000): gen-001 mean 20.6-40.7 ms per dispatch, stall rule without back-off 14.6-23.2 ms, final 0.07-0.2 ms vs a sleeping pool 0.07-0.14 ms; under ctest -j6 next to 16 busy threads (300 ms windows): no back-off 67-1177 us, final 84-149 us, sleeping pool 82-96 us. 1.1 s after the load stops, the pool's fastest dispatch is 4.0-4.5 us again (sleeping pool 35-46 us). Normal-load numbers unchanged by the back-off (32 threads 6-10 us, 16 threads 0.75-0.85 us). Counting workers' own idle-time preemption as overload was tried and dropped (made burst dispatches sleep-only: p50 55-60 us vs 7-18 us).

hypotheses_validated.claim: Workers left out of hx_pool_for_n regions now sleep spin_us after their own last task (hx_pool.h wording); dispatches without them no longer restart the window.
hypotheses_validated.evidence: 16-thread pool, spin_us=2000, back-to-back for_n(2) regions of 5 us: gen-001 12.8-15.8 CPUs busy, final 1.9-2.8 CPUs (process CPU time / wall time). test_pool asserts < nt/2.

hypotheses_validated.claim: test_pool timing checks are robust to concurrent runs: runs serialize on a lock file in the temp dir (owner pid; dead owner or >10 min old = taken over), and the 'workers sleep after spin_us' / 'slow tasks are not stalls' / for_n checks use process CPU time instead of latency.

open_questions: Quiet-machine target unverified: never fewer than ~7.6 other CPUs busy. At that load 32-thread dispatch mean 6.2-7.0 us vs 16-thread 0.76-0.84 us (~8x); under 85-90% load 6-10 us vs 0.75 us. With ~8 CPUs taken by other processes a 32-thread pool on 32 CPUs is oversubscribed, so this is not a quiet-machine number.

Native Linux untested (only WSL2, where the stall rescue works poorly and costs 1.1-1.3x at light load). Linux's balancer may refuse to migrate a recently-run (cache-hot) thread to an idle CPU, which would weaken the rescue there too; not verified.
